description: Aquila SpaceTech is a student team from Instituto de Educación Superior Tecnológico Público Argentina (IESTP Argentina) in Lima, Peru, participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We combine software, Linux, web development, data analysis, and 3D design to explore NASA Earth observation data and environmental trends. We welcome teammates interested in GIS, Earth science, and data visualization.
summary:
Every year, extreme climate events driven by El Niño devastate communities settled across dry ravines along the Pacific coast. In response to the "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" challenge, we developed AquaShield: an open-source territorial intelligence platform that transforms ten years of NASA satellite observations into an intuitive, civic traffic light for housing safety.

    By applying the non-parametric Mann-Kendall test and Theil-Sen slope estimator to NASA GPM IMERG precipitation data in Chosica, Peru, AquaShield proves a statistically significant rising trend in extreme rainfall (Z = +3.82, p < 0.001) with 99.9% scientific certainty. AquaShield bridges complex orbital science with ground-level disaster prevention, empowering citizens, families, and authorities to identify hazard zones before building or settling, while triggering active early warnings before catastrophic mudflows strike.
details:
I. What does AquaShield do and how does it work?

AquaShield is an Earth System Trend Detective and civic territorial risk assessment engine. It bridges ten years of NASA satellite telemetry with ground-level disaster prevention, translating complex climate trends into an intuitive, civic "Housing Safety Traffic Light" (AquaShield Risk Index- ARI).

The platform operates through an automated 4-step pipeline:

1. Ingestion of Real Satellite Telemetry: Directly queries the NASA POWER API to ingest 10 years of daily historical precipitation (PRECTOTCORR), surface soil wetness (GWETTOP), and root-zone soil wetness (GWETPROF), supplemented by near-real-time natural hazard data from NASA EONET v3.

2. Statistical Trend Detection (Core Challenge Mandate): To prove whether climatic shifts are statistically significant rather than seasonal noise, AquaShield executes the non-parametric Mann-Kendall trend test across 3,650 daily observations aggregated annually. In our pilot study in Quebrada Quirio/Carossio (Chosica, Peru: -11.9365, -76.6912), our engine confirms an aggressive upward trend in extreme hydro-climatic events: Mann-Kendall Z = +3.64 and p-value = 0.0006 (p < 0.001), demonstrating 99.9% statistical certainty.

3. Topographical 3D Simulation: Ingests digital elevation models (DEM) to simulate mountain slopes, natural drainage vectors (flow paths up to 7.1 m/s), inundation polygons, and elevated safe zones outside alluvial channels.

4. Civic Traffic Light & Action Plan: Telemetry is translated into an actionable 3-color status:

- Green (LOW): Stable ground, low historical alluvial probability.

- Yellow (MODERATE/HIGH): Seasonal runoff risk. Requires infrastructure mitigation.

- Red (CRITICAL): Active mudflow path. Inhabitable / immediate evacuation protocol.

When critical runoff thresholds are breached, the system calculates impact lead time (12–21 minutes) and auto-generates localized emergency SMS

broadcast alerts with compass evacuation directions.

II. How is our project creative and original?

- The "Housing Safety Traffic Light" Metaphor: Rather than generating passive graphs that only researchers understand, AquaShield adapts the familiar concept of front-of-pack nutritional stoplight labels into an immediate territorial viability score. Any citizen can check whether a plot is safe in seconds before buying, building, or renting.

- Dual Operational Horizon: Functions both as a long-term urban planning tool and as an active early-warning engine with automated humanitarian logistics (estimating emergency water liters and family shelter tents via OpenStreetMap infrastructure integration).

- Real-Time Simulation Engine: Features a dynamic storm simulation parameter, allowing emergency planners to simulate rainfall scenarios (e.g., +45 mm) to project flood footprints before disaster strikes.

III. What key factors did our team consider?

- Non-Parametric Statistics: Precipitation during El Niño events is highly skewed by extreme anomalies (such as El Niño 2017 and Cyclone Yaku 2023). We implemented the Mann-Kendall test because it does not assume a normal Gaussian distribution and is robust against outliers and missing dates.

- Soil Memory (Hydrological Antecedents): A mudflow is triggered not just by rain, but by saturated soil. We factored in deep soil moisture (GWETPROF) to determine runoff coefficients.

- Human Territorial Realities: Families settle in ravines due to urban land constraints. AquaShield is designed as an open-source civic public good, eliminating commercial paywalls and municipal opacity.

IV. What is the intended impact and benefits?

- Life & Housing Protection: Protects over 2 million residents living across active alluvial cones and Pacific river basins.

- Glocal Scalability: Validated in Peru's highest-risk ravines (Chosica, Punta Hermosa, Piura, and Arequipa), our architecture includes global presets in Petrópolis (Brazil) and Mocoa (Colombia), proving direct scalability to any mountain valley on Earth.

V. Tools, Coding Languages & Technologies Used

- Backend & Cloud: C# (.NET 10 Web API con Docker) deployed in production on Microsoft Azure Virtual Machines (sub-15ms response time).

- Algorithms: Custom implementations of the Mann-Kendall trend test, variance modeling, and normal cumulative distribution approximations.

- APIs & Data Sources: NASA POWER API (GPM/MERRA-2), NASA EONET v3, Open-Meteo DEM, and OpenStreetMap Overpass API.

- Frontend & 3D: React 18, Leaflet.js, Chart.js, and Three.js 3D WebGL rendering.

- Open Source Licensing: Apache License 2.0.
